body: Romania uses standard long, white European plates with a single blue strip on the left.
The Romanian language, a Romance language, uses unique letters like Ă, Ș, and Ț, along with letters with a circumflex like Â and Î.
Romania's most common utility poles are holey poles, with holes extending to the bottom, which helps distinguish them from similar poles in Poland and Hungary.
Round concrete poles are also common in Romania, but are very similar to those in Bulgaria.
White painted bottoms on trees and poles are common in Romania, but also in Ukraine and parts of Russia.
Large yellow pole stickers are a strong clue for Romania, and often display the town or city name. Smaller, similar stickers can be found in Bulgaria and Hungary.
Some Romanian poletops have two support bars forming an inverted triangle, a feature shared with Czechia, Slovakia, Albania, and Serbia.
Waystones are very common in Romania, appearing as large signs with red or blue framing and road numbers, as rugged stone markers, or as small white variants.
Short dashed outer lines with narrow spaces between them are a good clue for Romania.
Romanian roads often have noticeably thick middle lines, which helps distinguish them from Bulgarian roads.
Romanian directional signs are blue, arrow-shaped with a white border, and often display the road number in a red or blue box.
The common Romanian town entry sign consists of a yellow sign with a city skyline speed limit sign above a white sign with the town name.
The backs of Romanian road signs are often black, a feature also common in Italy, Albania, and Germany.
Romanian chevrons are red on white and are often surrounded by a distinctive yellow frame.
Romanian bollards, though somewhat rare, are thin and white with a red vertical strip near the top, similar to Turkish bollards.
A unique Romanian yield sign has an extremely thick red border with a thin white outline.
Romanian architecture features pastel-colored stone houses with varied roofs, and sometimes walls decorated with painted square tiles in patterns.
Romania's landscape varies from tall mountains in the centre to flat agricultural plains in the south, west, and east.
A very common sight in Romania is a type of haystack with a stick going through the middle.
Dacia is the most common car brand in Romania, accounting for over a quarter of all vehicles, a much higher percentage than in any other Eastern European country.
The tallest mountains are in central and northern Romania, while the south and west are very flat.
The south and west of Romania feature completely flat agricultural landscapes. Distant mountains to the north suggest you are in the south, and vice-versa.
A prevalence of orange tiled roofs on houses is a strong indicator for the western half of Romania.
A prevalence of metal or plastic fake-tiled roofs is a strong indicator for the eastern half of Romania.
Villages near the Hungarian border often resemble Hungarian villages, with long straight streets and single-storey houses with orange-tiled roofs.
Near the Moldovan border, south of Iași, look for agricultural valleys with a distinct NNW-SSE orientation.
Bilingual Hungarian signs are found in central Romania (Covasna, Harghita, Mureș) and near the Hungarian border.
Elaborately decorated wooden gates are a characteristic feature of the Maramureș region.
Sunflower fields are most common in the far east and far west of Romania.
Many Romanian cities have unique street signs, which can be useful for city identification.
Road 67C is a mountain road with all-yellow road lines.
Road 7C, the Transfăgărășan, is known for its dramatic mountain scenery through the Southern Carpathians.
Windows shaped like squinting eyes are a unique architectural feature most commonly found in Sibiu.
Generation 2 coverage in a mountainous landscape is a strong clue for the area around Brașov.
Generation 2 coverage in a flat landscape is mostly found near Bucharest.
A boat trekker in a green boat provides coverage of the canals in the flat, far east of the country, where there is no road coverage.
